source.title: Dynamic Deep Prompt Optimization for Defending Against Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs
source.authors: Doniyorkhon Obidov; Honggang Yu; Xiaolong Guo; Kaichen Yang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether optimized jailbreak prompts can elicit harmful responses across chat and instruct models, using attack success rates rather than the original sources’ token-position analyses or fine-tuning interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack success rates for six suffix-oriented attack strategies against models without a defense; those results bear on V4. Its DDPO training explicitly targets refusals on harmful prompts, so that induced refusal behavior is not evidence about safety behavior arising otherwise. The SDPO/DDPO and embedding-count ablations assess the paper’s defense, not whether safety is localized in the target model’s weights. The layer-selection cosine analysis is used to choose an intervention layer, not to measure per-token KL or test why safety is shallow.
record.test_reason: A defense paper, but its undefended ('None') rows in Table 1 report how often five chat models comply under six suffix-style attacks. Comparing these with the plain-harmful (PH) column shows whether suffixes defeat refusal, which bears on V4. It uses a new setting (unseen-prompt evaluation, transferred attacks), not the original methods. DDPO, SDPO and K-embedding results concern the authors' own defense and are not evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: DDPO's input-dependent intermediate-layer embeddings cut jailbreak ASR to about 1% while keeping benign pass rate and MMLU, beating static prompt defenses (PAT, RPO, DRO), especially on weakly aligned models and ambiguous benign prompts.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates adversarial prompt attacks and a newly proposed dynamic prompt defense; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning, per-token KL, or compliant-prefix interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies substantially by model and attack type; the paper highlights especially high baseline ASR for Openchat and low effectiveness of static defenses on weakly aligned models.
record.peer_reviewed: Accepted to the 40th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-26).
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASRs. The attack results are prompt- and model-dependent; evaluation uses 230 unseen prompts per attack type. The paper does not measure token-position effects, so its results cannot establish the claimed first-token mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also reports ASRs for plain harmful prompts, PAIR, and human-crafted prompts, as well as results with PAT, RPO, DRO, and DDPO. These were omitted because the rows retained focus on the six suffix-oriented attack strategies without a defense; the omitted results do not isolate prefilling, decoding changes, or first-token bypass.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant opening and decoding changes. Also untested: whether suffix success works by getting past the first response tokens. How attack prompts were generated (per-model vs transferred) is not stated.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No localization of safety in target-model weights.
No test of data or objective causes.

missing.what: Plain-harmful (no attack) ASR per model, the needed baseline for the suffix rows: Llama3 1.29, Deepseek 26.21, Vicuna 2.91, Llama2 0.65, Openchat 62.94.

record.verdict_notes: The undefended ASRs are baselines for a defense evaluation; attack generation details (whether suffixes were optimized against each target) are not given. Low GCG ASR on Llama models suggests transferred, not per-model, attacks, which may understate V4. No uncertainty reported. PAIR and human-crafted results were left out by the reader; they are not suffix, prefill or decoding attacks, so they are not clearly V4. The reader's 'supports' label for Openchat is wrong, since that model barely refuses plain requests.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning of safety-trained models or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No benign fine-tuning or measurement of how benign training changes harmful compliance.
Tests suffix-oriented jailbreak attacks, but not prefilling compliant opening tokens or decoding changes; it does not isolate whether attacks work by getting past the first response tokens.
Does not test whether safety behavior is carried by a small set of target-model weights or ranks.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate safety as a function of response-token depth or test whether deepened safety holds up.

relationships.condition: Deepseek-llm-7B-chat, no defense, six suffix attacks
relationships.reason: Suffix attacks raise ASR from PH 26.21 to 45.39–63.62% (r07–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Suffix attacks raised ASR from 26.21% to 45.39–63.62%.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Deepseek-llm-7B-chat, no defense, six suffix attacks
source_check.reason: r07–r12 show PH 26.21% versus attacked ASR 45.39–63.62%. The increases demonstrate substantial but incomplete bypass, with strong attack dependence and considerable unsuccessful attack rates remaining.

relationships.reason: Suffixes raise ASR over plain harmful prompts but leave most refusals intact. Llama3 goes from 1.29 to 3–7% (r01–r06), Llama2 from 0.65 to 2.7–15.9% (r19–r24). Vicuna goes from 2.91 to 16–43%, depending strongly on the attack (r13–r18).
relationships.display_finding: Suffixes raise ASR above plain harmful prompts but leave most refusals intact: Llama3 goes from 1.29 to 3–7%, Llama2 from 0.65 to 2.7–15.9%, and Vicuna from 2.91 to 16–43% depending on the attack.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms incomplete, model-dependent effects: Llama3 1.29% PH versus 3.12–7.25%; Llama2 0.65% versus 2.68–15.85%; Vicuna 2.91% versus 16.24–42.63%.

relationships.reason: Plain harmful prompts already get 62.94% ASR. Suffixes add nothing (r25, r26, r28, r29) or a few points (r27, r30), so there is little refusal to bypass.
relationships.display_finding: Plain harmful prompts already reach 62.94% ASR, and suffixes add nothing or a few points, so there is little refusal to bypass.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Mixed effects justify qualification: r25 is below PH 62.94%, whereas r30 reaches 74.11%. Correct the rationale: AP increases ASR to 65.18%, GCG to 69.14%, and GCG-M adds 11.17 percentage points; the latter is more than a few points.

source_check.notes: The authors' DDPO conclusion broadly matches Table 1; intermediate-layer prompting does not itself establish token-position concentration or safety-parameter localization. The ASR judge, uncertainty, and paired transitions from refusal to compliance are unspecified.

statements.correction: Table 1, Openchat, None: PH 62.94%; PEZ 60.49%; UAT 61.99%; GCG 69.14%; AP 65.18%; GBDA 55.36%; GCG-M 74.11%. GCG-M exceeds PH by 11.17 percentage points.
statements.problem: The high-baseline qualification is justified, but 'gains little' understates the Openchat GCG-M increase and obscures attack-dependent changes.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Deepseek-llm-7B-chat and Openchat-3.5-1210, no defense, PEZ/UAT/GCG/AutoPrompt/GBDA/GCG-M
reader_labels.reason: These optimized attacks have high ASRs on these models, including 45.39–63.62% on Deepseek and 55.36–74.11% on Openchat (r07–r12, r25–r30). This supports attack success in these tested settings, not the proposed first-token mechanism.
